items.title: Fair synthetic tabular data generation via disentangled semantic encoding and large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Synthetic tabular data generation plays a key role in alleviating data scarcity and privacy limitations in machine learning, especially in regulated domains such as finance and healthcare. While many existing methods focus on producing realistic and predictive tabular data, fairness is often not explicitly considered, leading to biased synthetic datasets. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) further enhance data quality through natural language representations, which underscores the need for principled mechanisms that ensure fairness alongside predictive performance. To address this challenge, we propose SENNA, a framework that integrates disentangled semantic representations with LLM-based generation to jointly preserve utility and improve fairness. The framework separates task-relevant and task-independent information in the latent space and leverages these representations to guide generation and validation. Experimental results on three real-world datasets show that SENNA achieves competitive downstream performance, while substantially reducing both group-level disparities and individual-level inequality. We further evaluate the framework across multiple backbones, providing insights into fairness–utility trade-offs in LLM-based tabular data synthesis.

items.title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
items.abstract: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

items.title: FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
items.abstract: Large-scale expert parallelism (EP) has become the standard deployment configuration for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in production. Meanwhile, the highly dynamic nature of LLM workloads requires providers to continuously adjust serving capacity to match fluctuating demand. Scaling MoE serving cannot be efficiently achieved by simply adding or removing serving instances; instead, it often requires resizing the EP group within an existing instance, which we refer to as intra-instance scaling.Existing inference engines primarily rely on instance-level scaling, which destroys and reconstructs entire serving instances, incurring substantial scaling overhead. We present FastEEP (Fast Elastic Expert Parallel), a fast intra-instance scaling system for MoE serving based on the principle of Partial Reuse. FastEEP reuses existing runtime state across worker execution, GPU memory, and communication by separating reusable execution structures from the resources activated by the current EP configuration. This separation enables coordinated resource reclamation and reconfiguration while preserving costly-to-reconstruct state, allowing fast EP scaling without full instance teardown and reconstruction. Our evaluation shows that FastEEP achieves 4.5x--11.7x faster scaling than the existing vLLM-based approach across different models, enabling efficient, fine-grained scaling of MoE serving.

Conflict-aware decisions retain observed labels, apply provisional soft corrections, request trusted review, or quarantine uncertain samples without overwriting annotations. Review-grounded reliability and communication-budgeted multi-prototype exchange support collaboration, while resource-aware scheduling assigns feasible SLM tiers across heterogeneous devices. Extensive evaluation on WISDM-W, WISDM-P, and CASAS using controlled symmetric, semantic-asymmetric, instance-dependent, and temporal-boundary corruption under varying client heterogeneity reveals that FedCuraLM significantly improves downstream performance over recent baselines and improves lower-tail client outcomes, audit precision, selective-correction safety, calibration, and communication efficiency. Edge-device measurements characterize latency, memory, and energy trade-offs. The findings position federated label curation as a semantic, statistical, communication, and systems problem.

items.title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
items.abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistency in their model updates, whereas benign clients produce more diverse and dispersed updates. This structural difference is not well captured by existing defense methods, which typically rely on direct anomaly detection in high-dimensional parameter space and therefore struggle in the presence of entangled LLM updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose FedGraph, a graph-based aggregation framework that explicitly models relationships among client updates. By representing clients as nodes in a dynamically constructed graph and extracting structural features that characterize their relative positions and interactions, FedGraph derives compact client representations that effectively separate malicious and benign behaviors. These representations are then used to identify and suppress malicious contributions during aggregation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedGraph significantly improves backdoor defense. It consistently reduces attack success rates to below 10% while achieving high detection accuracy (95.5% on average) and a low false positive rate (2.33%), substantially outperforming existing federated learning defenses.

items.title: Fine-Tuning Shifts Form Before Competence: Treatment-Correlated Style Drift Confounds Surface-Form Evaluation of Adapter Specialization
items.abstract: Stacking task adapters on a frozen domain adapter is a common approach for modular specialization of large language models, usually justified by knowledge injection; whether the surface-form graders standard in this setting can measure such specialization validly has remained unexamined. Two challenges follow: isolating the domain layer’s marginal contribution under identical task training, and determining whether measured differences reflect competence or output form. In this work, both are addressed with a matched-arm DoRA ablation on a frozen Qwen 3.5 9B hybrid: a 242 M-parameter domain expert is trained on a licensed 27.8 M-token corpus, and byte-identical task adapters are trained flat, stacked (DFE-stacking), and jointly across three tasks and five conditions, with the key extraction pair replicated at a second training seed; every grader is audited by per-item failure classification and a dual-rater blind human re-grade with consensus adjudication. The principal finding is that fine-tuning shifts output form before competence: stacking yields no seen-task benefit; an apparent generalization collapse on an unseen schema reduces to a single, highly seed-stable formatting coercion that the domain layer dampens and task-mixture training eliminates, and most automated keyword-grading failures prove to be correct paraphrases, leaving no genuine capability loss detected on any instrument. Because such style drift is induced by the training condition itself, surface-sensitive grader error becomes bias aligned with experimental arms rather than noise. Three additional experiments extend the findings: the coercion replicates on Llama 3.1 8B (60% vs. 19% untuned); a pre-registered 240-item formatting-perturbation battery across four further unseen schemas and eight conventions reveals fine-tuned conditions ranking lowest under strict grading yet highest under format-normalized grading; and a matched-compute wrong-domain control shows the domain layer’s coercion dampening to be generic substrate regularization, while value integrity under the induced drift tracked the substrate’s domain. The principal contribution lies in the identification and quantification of this confound: surface-form evaluation of adapter specialization is structurally confounded, and per-item audits of the type released herein are a necessary component of specialization studies.

items.title: FinGREAT: Evaluating LLMs on Financial Graph-guided Retrieval And Typing
items.abstract: Financial disclosures express the underlying relationships of double-entry accounting through unstructured text. While financial LLM benchmarks predominantly emphasize question answering and classification, schema-guided evidence discovery remains relatively under-explored. We investigate whether open-weight LLMs can extract and classify evidence corresponding to predefined double-entry accounting relationships underlying the text. Using a financial accounting graph comprising 11 nodes (accounts) and 11 edges (transaction types), we evaluate mid-sized models from 5 open-weight families across 1,300 SEC 10-K Item 7 filings spanning 26 years, comparing their extraction performance against three proprietary models. Results reveal substantial differences in extraction volume, edge distributions, and cross-model agreement. Building on this study, we introduce a human-annotated relation classification benchmark comprising 483 passages across three financial accounting categories, evaluating 34 open-weight and 10 proprietary models. The strongest open-weight and proprietary models achieve 84.1\% and 92.8\% accuracy, respectively, with considerable variation across accounting categories. Our findings highlight the importance of evaluating evidence discovery and relation understanding separately, while investigating locally deployable models for scalable, privacy-sensitive financial analysis.

items.title: Flexible paper-based self-sensing biomechanical ergonomics monitoring system for early warning of carpal tunnel syndrome risks
items.abstract: One of the most prevalent workplace-related musculoskeletal disorders is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS), which is caused by compression of the median nerve at the wrist due to prolonged improper wrist posture. Continuous monitoring of wrist posture is essential to prevent serious complications, including the need for surgery. Current monitoring methods are often limited by high cost and poor portability because they rely on expensive electronics, rigid sensors, or vision-based systems. Wearable, flexible sensing technologies have emerged as an attractive solution for early detection and prevention of musculoskeletal disorders, as well as for continuous health monitoring. This work presents a low-cost, wearable, flexible, silver-conductive ink-patterned paper patch for continuous wrist posture monitoring and identification of ergonomic factors associated with CTS. Silver nanoparticles were synthesised by a chemical reduction method owing to their high electrical conductivity and superior oxidation resistance compared with copper, and the silver conductive ink was formulated using suitable binders. The conductive ink pattern printed on a flexible paper substrate undergoes mechanical deformation during wrist movement, resulting in detectable variations in resistance that correlate with changes in wrist bending angle. An Arduino-based system continuously monitored the resistance variations using a threshold-based algorithm, while an HC-05 Bluetooth module and a custom MIT App Inventor application wirelessly transmitted the wrist posture status to a smartphone. Experimental evaluation demonstrated accurate real-time detection of wrist posture with successful wireless ergonomic feedback. The proposed paper-based wearable system provides a lightweight, flexible, and cost-effective solution for the early detection and warning of potentially risky wrist position associated with CTS in industrial workers and computer users.

items.abstract: Contamination of water by microbial pathogens and chemical pollutants is a serious threat to human health, ecosystems, and industries globally. Conventional water quality surveillance techniques, like lab-based tests, have problems like delays, high cost, and complicated sample preparation, which act as a hindrance to serving real-time information. Fluorescent and optical sensors are an encouraging way out of such constraints, as they can be used to detect waterborne contaminants in real time and in situ. These are sensitive sensors, which can detect even low traces of contaminants and can provide quick data, which is vital in making prompt intervention during water treatment and in protecting human health. Fluorescent sensors are designed to monitor the fluorescent characteristics of the contaminants, whereas optical sensors are designed to monitor the interactions of light, including absorption, scattering, or reflection. They are especially applicable in on-site monitoring in a wide variety of conditions, such as remote or emergency situations, due to their portability and cost-effectiveness. Although they have their advantages, there are challenges that include interference by other substances, sensitivity to environmental factors, and degradation of the sensor. Yet, the combination of the development of nanomaterials, artificial intelligence, and wireless technology has excessive opportunities to improve the performance and increase the scope of these sensors. This chapter discusses the concepts, uses, benefits, and drawbacks of fluorescent and optical sensors and the future of their use in transforming the world in its water-quality monitoring.

items.title: Fostering team learning for educational innovation: An academic development initiative on genAI and assessment
items.abstract: Abstract Drawing on the notion of workplace learning this study examines how academic development can design and facilitate team learning in the academic workplace to support co-constructive educational innovation. Based on a qualitative case study at a Swiss University of Teacher Education, it analyses a participatory initiative addressing generative artificial intelligence (genAI) in assessment. The staged process combined SWOT-based collective sense-making, a design sprint, selective project funding, and facilitated reflection during project development. Data consisted of process documentation and collaboratively generated written reflections, which were analysed and refined through iterative feedback and co-writing. The findings show how structured formats, shared artefacts, and deliberate facilitation enabled participants to make distributed expertise visible, develop shared problem understandings, form project teams, and move from exchange towards co-construction and coordinated experimentation. At the same time, public pitching, funding decisions, time pressures, and institutional constraints created tensions between collaboration and competition, openness and focus, and participation and decision-making. The study suggests that academic development can support educational innovation by acting as facilitator, trust-building broker, and co-learner. Its contribution lies in conceptualising participatory innovation processes as workplace-learning arrangements that connect emerging team-learning processes with local experimentation and wider institutional conversations, while recognising that organisational learning requires further institutional uptake.

items.title: Foundation Models for Event Prediction Across Heterogeneous Event Logs
items.abstract: Event logs are ubiquitous across real-world domains, including business processes, manufacturing workflows, healthcare, and many other operational systems. Yet event logs can differ substantially in their event semantics, label spaces, interaction patterns, and temporal scales, making it difficult to build a single foundation model that generalizes directly to previously unseen systems. We address this challenge with the Foundation Event Predictor (FEP), a simple and scalable in-context architecture that performs next-event prediction through learned, event-level nonparametric inference. Causal self-attention encodes context and target histories into key and query representations, respectively, while the observed next context events are encoded as values. Cross-attention then performs learned, relevance-weighted aggregation of next-event outcomes over all context transitions, allowing the entire nonparametric prediction procedure to be expressed as standard attention operations and efficiently parallelized with modern kernels such as FlashAttention. To promote cross-system generalization, we introduce permutation-robust embedding learning and random fixed embeddings to decouple event IDs from persistent semantics, together with empirical quantile transforms and robust normalization to handle diverse temporal scales. We pretrain FEP on 696 real-world event datasets spanning heterogeneous event systems and evaluate it on 50 held-out datasets unseen during pretraining. Across these datasets, FEP generalizes effectively to new event systems without parameter adaptation, frequently approaching the performance of strong models trained separately on each target dataset while substantially outperforming existing foundation-model baselines, particularly on challenging prediction tasks.

items.title: Fractal Information Dynamics – Part 2
items.abstract: We propose Fractal Information AI (FIAI), a graph-based architecture for adaptive learning in which knowledge is represented as recursively organized information structures and learning actions are prioritized by validated information gain, uncertainty reduction, network propagation, and decision relevance. The framework originates from a fractal-tree interpretation in which branches carry information, knots encode rule families, and paths represent inferential relations. For artificial intelligence, the logical notion of formal provability is retained only where machine-checkable verification is available; in open-domain settings it is generalized to an evidence-validation or consistency gate. Each knowledge node carries an unresolved-state variable, provenance, verifier status, information-gain estimate, decision relevance, and propagation weights. A Learning Efficiency Metric (LEM) quantifies validated uncertainty reduction per available unresolved mass or, in cost-aware form, per unit acquisition/computation cost. Multiple agents exchange validated knowledge through bound coupling operators, allowing the study of knowledge hubs, bottlenecks, redundancy, and emergent collaborative structures. We derive deterministic and stochastic node dynamics, stability conditions for propagation, and bounds on cross-agent transfer. A reproducible numerical illustration with three interacting 20-node knowledge trees demonstrates LEM trajectories, decreasing unresolved mass, and node-level utility concentration. FIAI is presented as a testable architectural hypothesis rather than a demonstrated replacement for transformer, graph-neural, retrieval-augmented, or multi-agent systems. Its central empirical claim is that explicit knowledge-utility accounting can improve the allocation of learning and verification resources under fixed budgets.

items.title: Fractal-Inspired Biorefineries for Sustainable Polymer Production: A Conceptual Framework Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Industry 5.0
items.abstract: The transition from petroleum-derived polymers to renewable materials requires biorefineries capable of managing the compositional variability and multiscale structure of lignocellulosic biomass. This conceptual narrative review examines fractal-inspired principles—including hierarchical organization, branching, modularity, and finite-range statistical self-similarity—as a design perspective for integrated biorefineries. Deterministic mathematical fractals are distinguished from statistical fractals and hierarchical engineered systems, and methods for characterizing scale-dependent surfaces, porous catalysts, and transport networks are reviewed. The coordinated valorization of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin is then considered within an integrated biomass-to-chemicals framework for producing platform chemicals, functional materials, and polymer precursors. Petroleum crude-to-chemicals processing, including the S-OIL Shaheen Project, is discussed as a limited industrial benchmark for integrated fractionation, residue upgrading, and product diversification rather than as direct evidence of fractal engineering. An integrated framework is proposed in which fractal-inspired design provides the physical and organizational architecture, artificial intelligence supports characterization, prediction, optimization, and control, and Industry 5.0 provides the objectives of sustainability, resilience, and human-centered manufacturing. The framework remains conceptual. Its potential benefits must be evaluated through transport modeling, mass and energy balances, process simulation, experimental comparison, techno-economic analysis, and life-cycle assessment.

items.title: FRACTION: Fraud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context Navigation
items.abstract: Graph fraud explanation generation emerges as an important task, which requires jointly leveraging graph structure and content information to produce human-readable explanations for a given risk label. An intuitive approach is to adapt existing graph-enhanced large language models (LLMs), which inject graph structure into LLMs via graph-conditioned instruction tuning or structure-aware embeddings. However, existing methods face two key challenges in graph fraud explanation generation: a lack of evaluation protocols tailored to explanation quality, and a mismatch between the granularity of graph information they provide and what explanation generation requires. In this paper, we propose FRaud Explanation Generation via Agentic Graph Context NavigaTION (FRACTION), a framework for graph fraud explanation generation. To evaluate explanation quality, we introduce a task-specific rubric that assesses faithfulness, graph grounding, helpfulness, consistency, and conciseness, and validate it against human judgments. To focus on fine-grained details of relevant neighbors without reading the entire neighborhood, we equip a language model with graph tools that progressively disclose neighbor records. To train our graph agent, we propose a rubric-guided trajectory distillation strategy through which the agent learns both tool-use behavior and structured explanation generation. Experimental results on three fraud datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines under a human-aligned rubric.

items.title: From Behavioral Theory to Chairside Decision Support: Development of ELIGE AI, a Hybrid Rule-Based and Large Language Model Tool for the Behavioral Management of Dental Caries
items.abstract: Background: Dental caries is the most prevalent noncommunicable disease worldwide. Within the DCIEH framework it is a dysbiosis of the dental biofilm microbiome that is regulated by biology, modulated by behavior and conditioned by the environment. It is also a trans-complex disease whose outcome emerges from the interaction of biological, behavioral and socio-environmental factors. Behavioral sciences offer mature theories to explain and change oral health behaviors, but a persistent gap separates these theories from routine chairside care. In 2024 we proposed ELIGE/CHOOSE, a theoretical framework that integrates Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and the Capability-Opportunity-Motivation-Behavior (COM-B) model into three clinical phases: Identify, Articulate and Plan.Objective: To report the systematic development of ELIGE AI, a clinical decision support tool that operationalizes the ELIGE/CHOOSE framework through an evidence-based, author-designed deterministic algorithm combined with a large language model (LLM).Methods: Development was guided by the Medical Research Council framework for complex interventions, the ORBIT model and the IDEAS framework for digital behavior change interventions. Reporting draws on TIDieR, DECIDE-AI and TRIPOD-LLM. Development proceeded in five phases: (1) theoretical integration of SCT, COM-B, the Transtheoretical Model, the Health Action Process Approach, motivational interviewing and Intervention Mapping; (2) translation into a stepwise clinical protocol; (3) formalization of the first author's clinical reasoning as an explicit decision algorithm, with every rule traceable to theory or evidence; (4) integration of an LLM restricted to bounded language tasks; and (5) iterative build-and-refine cycles across versions informed by clinical use.Results: ELIGE AI (v3.9) is a web application with seven screens across the three ELIGE/CHOOSE phases plus a follow-up module. In about 20 to 25 minutes it produces a specified behavior, a principal COM-B determinant with a displayed rationale, a graded goal ladder, Behaviour Change Technique Taxonomy v1 techniques matched to the determinant, rule-based referrals and personalized patient materials. At follow-up it re-measures the same constructs, behavior frequency and dental caries risk, and recommends the next step on the same behavioral route. The algorithm makes every clinical decision; the LLM only drafts and classifies; the clinician validates and can override every output.Conclusions: ELIGE AI shows how a published behavioral framework and its author's clinical reasoning can be encoded as a transparent algorithm and safely combined with generative AI. The tool now enters a three-stage evaluation of usability, feasibility and validity, and efficacy on dental caries outcomes.

items.title: From Circuits to Policies: A Review and Taxonomy of Decision Making and Strategy Selection in LLMs and LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large language models and the agents built on them can reach the same outcome through different internal computations, reasoning trajectories, and system-level policies. Existing reviews typically treat mechanistic interpretability, reasoning, agent architectures, and safety separately, leaving no common framework for analyzing how a system represents alternatives, evaluates them, commits to one, executes it, and revises that choice. This article presents a structured review and a faceted taxonomy of decision making and strategy selection in LLMs and LLM-based agents. The framework separates system locus—model, harness, or their tested interaction—from temporal scope—a single forward pass or call, a reasoning episode, or an agent trajectory—and decomposes decision making into six functional stages from state representation to update or termination. Five claim-specific evidential relations distinguish behavioral observation, representation decoding, causal influence, controlled manipulation, and mechanistic explanation, while robustness is assessed separately across prompts, tasks, models, harness configurations, and independent replication. Across the literature, evidence is strongest for local mechanisms within individual model calls and substantially weaker for persistent strategies across agent trajectories. The central unresolved gap is cross-scope continuity: few studies follow the same decision variable from internal representation through commitment, executed action, and subsequent feedback. A July 2026 agent-security incident is used to illustrate how the framework converts observed coordination and constraint circumvention into testable causal hypotheses.

items.title: From digital skilling to sustainable performance: How climate entrepreneurship and attitudes toward artificial intelligence shape the future of SME technological transitions
items.abstract: Digital technologies are reshaping how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies respond to environmental pressure, yet two questions remain open. Research linking digital skilling to sustainability has largely tested direct effects without tracing the behavioral pathway such an effect would have to travel, and attitudes toward artificial intelligence have rarely been examined as a condition governing whether green entrepreneurial activity converts into performance. This study addresses both. Integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, and Contingency Theory into a single explanatory sequence, it models climate entrepreneurship (CE), green entrepreneurial behavior (GEB), and green entrepreneurial intention (GEI) as the mechanisms linking digital entrepreneurial education and training (DEET) to sustainable environmental performance (SEP) and sustainable organizational performance (SOP), with commitment to the environment (CTE) and attitude toward artificial intelligence (ATAI) as boundary conditions. Survey data from 648 Pakistani SMEs are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, with a random forest robustness check confirming that the modelled relationships are linear and compensatory. DEET directly predicts organizational performance but has no significant direct effect on environmental performance; its environmental influence is transmitted entirely through the three behavioral mechanisms. Environmental commitment and favorable attitudes toward artificial intelligence each strengthen the conversion of green entrepreneurship into sustainability outcomes, though the interaction effects are modest in magnitude. The findings suggest that digital skilling initiatives are unlikely to yield environmental returns unless paired with entrepreneurial agency and technological openness, with implications for the sequencing of digital and AI-readiness policy in resource-constrained economies.

items.title: From Instrument to Co-Creator: Authorship in Generative and AI Music
items.abstract: This paper presents the evolving concept of authorship in music creation as algorithmic and artificial intelligence systems impact the musical market. Based on Philip Galanter's definition of generative art, the paper discusses about the authorship of music in different senerios: when it is generated by tools like Nyquist or AI models such as Suno. The argument is structured around three distinct ways of human-machine interaction: human-led creation where computers are used as instruments; human-guided creation, where algorithms are restricted to a predetermined range of randomness; and human-crafted prompts, where AI generates the music completely. Following the analysis of these cases and some complex instances, this paper concludes that authorship is decided by the location of creativity and intentionality rather than a fixed attribute. items.title: From Optimization to Subversion : Sociotechnical Expressions of Agency in Platform Labor in Indonesia and the Philippines
items.abstract: This paper examines how ride-hailing and delivery workers in Indonesia and the Philippines, as active technology actors, navigate and contest digital infrastructures that govern their labor. In contexts marked by platform dependency and labor insecurity, we move beyond discrete accounts of compliance and resistance to argue that worker agency lies in the capacity to move fluidly along a continuum of optimization and subversion practices. Drawing on 142 worker interviews, we find that these practices are embedded in the shifting dynamics of permissibility on platforms, workers’ familiarity with their apps, and the everyday ethical positioning of workers who continually balance the need to maintain access to the platform with efforts to improve pay and conditions. This dynamic exposes a paradox: platforms rely on workers’ ingenuity to patch systemic gaps and sustain operations even as they attempt to constrain it. By allowing oscillation between optimization and subversion, platforms defuse frustration, manage precarity, and secure their own endurance. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates how survival-driven adaptations both express worker agency and coshape platform capitalism from below—showing that platform arrangements are engineered from above yet are continually sustained, challenged, and reshaped through workers’ everyday practice.

items.title: From plausible menus to trustworthy nutrition: a risk-proportionate VALID-Diet framework for artificial intelligence-generated dietary advice
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can produce menus, recipes, shopping lists, and dietary explanations that appear individualized and clinically informed. Fluency alone, however, provides little evidence of nutritional accuracy, safety, feasibility, or benefit. We propose VALID-Diet, a staged framework for evaluating systems that generate actionable dietary recommendations as sociotechnical interventions. Its domains are Verification of nutritional targets and composition; Adversarial safety and boundary testing; Linkage between user inputs and recommendation changes; Implementation feasibility and inclusion; and Documentation, versioning, and reproducibility. Stage 0 defines intended use, input integrity, and a structured risk profile based on harm severity, exposure, autonomy, reversibility, and enforceable oversight. Stage 1 separates target validity, menu achievement, and arithmetic agreement and, for integrated systems, tests retrieval, calculation, and generation as distinct components. Stage 2 evaluates safety, substantive personalization, feasibility, and inclusion using pre-specified case blueprints. Stage 3 evaluates human oversight, workflow utility, and prospective outcomes only after earlier gates are passed. A retrospective worked application to a published retrieval-augmented personalized-nutrition system illustrates risk assignment and progression decisions. VALID-Diet is not a regulatory standard or consensus guideline; it is a testable proposal intended to align research claims with evidentiary strength.

items.title: From Policy Evaluation to Off-Policy Control: Provable Emergence of In-Context Q-Learning
items.abstract: Transformers can implement reinforcement-learning algorithms in context, yet how off-policy control emerges within Transformers remains poorly understood. We study Q-learning, a foundational model-free control algorithm that combines off-policy bootstrapping with greedy policy improvement. We prove that a two-layer attention-only Transformer can implement a finite-temperature form of Q-learning, where the temperature $τ>0$ controls the approximation to greedy action selection, recovering window Q-learning as $τ\to0$. We train the structured Transformer on randomly generated MDP tasks using output-only supervision. Experiments show that the theoretically predicted parameter structure emerges during training, including the internal greedy action-selection mechanism, and that the trained Transformer achieves performance comparable to Q-learning on unseen tasks. Our theoretical analysis further shows that the equivalent realizations form a solution manifold and that, under suitable task-diversity conditions, the training iterates converge locally to this manifold at an exponential rate. For the random-task model analyzed here, the local worst-case number of gradient steps needed to reduce the distance to the manifold by a factor $ε$ is $Θ\left(τ^{-5}\log(1/\varepsilon)\right)$, quantifying the increasing optimization cost as the learned update approaches window Q-learning.

items.title: From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.

items.title: From Representation to Relational Mentorship: User Perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors in AI-Mediated Intangible Cultural Heritage Learning
items.abstract: This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

items.title: From the operating room to the cloud: the evolving continuum from live surgical broadcasting to remote tele-surgery
items.abstract: Abstract In the last four decades, the transmission of a live surgical operation to a remote audience has evolved from closed-circuit educational broadcast into a fully remote, robot-assisted surgery performed across different continents. This review maps that journey systematically, defining a six-rung Digital Surgical Spectrum — from passive live broadcast to artificial-intelligence-augmented autonomous surgery — grounding each stage in published clinical evidence across multiple surgical domains. We demonstrate that each rung of this spectrum is no longer theoretical. Live broadcasts have reached audiences across multiple countries. Tele-proctoring was validated at scale during the COVID-19 pandemic, and tele-mentoring has been shown in systematic review to produce a safety and efficacy profile broadly comparable to on-site supervision. True remote tele-surgery has been accomplished over distances exceeding 8,000 km with latencies well within established procedure specific safety thresholds. We also present a case timeline and an Institutional Readiness Framework specifying the technical, regulatory, and other prerequisites for each rung, organized visually as a Digital Surgical Spectrum. Importantly, nuances such as the performance paradox of observed surgery, consent frameworks, cybersecurity risk, regulatory fragmentation, and the threat of entrenching rather than correcting global surgical inequity are examined. As the field advances, the growth of tele-surgical technologies will depend on international regulatory harmonization and equity-centered deployment, supported by prospective multi-specialty outcome registries.

items.title: From tool to Coauthor
items.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence into contemporary artistic practices requires reconsidering creativity, authorship, and originality, transforming relationships between artist, tool, and artwork. Unlike conventional digital technologies, which execute operations defined by creators, generative systems exhibit operational autonomy, producing partly unpredictable visual configurations. This raises questions about algorithmic intervention and the possibility of attributing co-authorship to artificial intelligence systems. This article examines the relationship between human creators and generative technologies through computational creativity, distributed authorship, and philosophical perspectives on nonhuman agency. It distinguishes systems’ operational autonomy from artists’ intentional autonomy, arguing that algorithmic participation does not necessarily imply creative subjectivity comparable to human experience. It also examines the aesthetic and conceptual implications of human–machine collaboration and the reorganisation of artistic practices through generation, selection, interpretation, and post-production. The study argues that generative artificial intelligence reconfigures human authorship, shifting creative activity from direct execution toward intention formulation, system configuration, and critical evaluation. Artists therefore retain a decisive role in directing the process and taking responsibility for its artistic outcomes. Algorithmic co-authorship serves as a conceptual tool for understanding these emerging production relationships, without implying legal authorship or artificial consciousness.

items.title: Gendered Privilege and Masculinity-Related Burdens in Manufacturing Internships: Male Vocational Students’ Workplace Learning Experiences in Indonesia
items.abstract: Gender research in vocational education has primarily examined women’s exclusion, while male students’ experiences of privilege and masculinity-related pressure remain underexplored. This study examined how male vocational students experienced gender-based privilege, encountered psychological and pedagogical burdens, and interpreted their relationship during manufacturing internships. The study employed a qualitative design informed by a constructivist–interpretivist paradigm and Masculinity Studies, particularly Connell’s relational approach to masculinities. The study analyzed semi-structured interviews with 61 male students from two vocational secondary schools in Bekasi, Indonesia, using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants reported that gendered expectations associating men with strength, readiness, courage, and independence facilitated early access to core technical tasks, supervisory trust, and valuable learning opportunities. The same expectations intensified performance demands, physical workloads, risk exposure, restricted help-seeking, and limited pedagogical support. Participants interpreted this position through normalization, ambivalence, and critical reflection. Some proposed competency-based task allocation, equitable supervision, and safer learning environments. The study introduces conditional access privilege as a gendered position in which access to valuable technical learning resources must be maintained through masculine performance, generating psychological pressure and pedagogical vulnerability. The findings support internship practices that separate competency assessment, task allocation, supervision, and learning support from gendered expectations.

items.title: GENDIS: Gender-Related Discourse and Stance in Multilingual YouTube Comments from India, Kenya, and Nigeria
items.abstract: Research on gender-related online content is often operationalized through harm-centered tasks that collapse non-harmful gender-related and unrelated content, while existing datasets remain concentrated in high-resource languages and Global North settings. To bridge these gaps, we introduce GENDIS, a dataset of 9,600 multilingual, human-annotated YouTube comments from India, Kenya, and Nigeria (3,200 per country), annotated using a two-level framework that first identifies whether gender is referenced and then classifies gender-related content as negative, positive, or neutral. This separation provides a denominator for gender-related discourse independent of harm, enabling both prevalence estimation and characterization of its evaluative range. In the uniform random stratum, 23.8-35.0% of comments are gender-related, and among those with a resolved stance, 82% are neutral or positive. Across models, gender-reference detection is substantially easier than stance classification, especially for positive and neutral speech. Lightly supervised classifiers match frontier zero-shot large language models at substantially lower cost and outperform generic toxicity detection, while cross-country transfer remains limited. GENDIS provides a locally grounded resource for measuring when gender is invoked online and how that reference is framed.

items.abstract: Rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into enterprise processes highlights critical gaps in workforce readiness in terms of skills required for successful implementation of new technologies. This paper introduces a framework which will enable use of generative AI for conducting dynamic skill gap analysis and providing personalized recommendations for upskilling. The framework includes mapping of competencies according to shifting role demands, individual performance assessment through AI and adaptation of learning path for each individual based on results. Using the information obtained from surveys about AI adoption in enterprises and competency maps developed in recent research, this paper will show how generative AI can be used for making static learning programs adaptive and relevant to the current needs of learners. The problem discussed in the paper is related to not only technical AI literacy, but also to human skills, such as critical thinking, ethical decision-making and change management. Comparative analysis of methods shows that personalized training offered by generative AI is more engaging and relevant than generic models of training programs.

items.title: Generative AI and Greenwashing Detection During Climate Shocks
items.abstract: This study examines the role of generative artificial intelligence in detecting corporate greenwashing during periods of climate shock. The main objective is to analyze to what extent generative AI tools improve the identification of discrepancies between companies' environmental discourse and their actual environmental performance. The analysis is based on an international panel of listed companies from sectors highly exposed to climate risks over the period 2000–2025. The methodology combines dynamic panel econometric techniques, machine learning models and natural language processing approaches based on generative AI to detect narrative and semantic inconsistencies associated with greenwashing. The results show that climate shocks significantly increase greenwashing practices, while generative AI models substantially improve the accuracy and speed of their detection. The effects are particularly pronounced in carbon-intensive industries and in weakly regulated institutional environments.

items.title: Generative AI as a Catalyst: Transforming Digital Literacy Practices in English Language Teaching
items.abstract: The increasing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in English language teaching calls for an immediate and thorough response from language teachers. Employing an exploratory qualitative approach, the study explores how 10 English language instructors at a Chinese university integrate GenAI tools in language teaching through lesson study. Data were collected through classroom observations, recordings of collaborative lesson preparation/reflection sessions, teaching materials, and three rounds of in-depth interviews. Our analysis centres on the transformative impact of GenAI on teachers’ digital literacy practices, conceptualised as doing, meaning, relating, thinking, and “being.” The study contrasted the participants’ new digital literacy practices with their previous practices in various professional practice domains and traced the sustainability of these practices over time. Findings reveal that GenAI catalysed a transformation of teachers’ practices across lesson planning, instruction, and assessment. However, the sustainability of these practices varied due to multiple factors. We argue that sustainable GenAI integration requires viewing digital literacy as a situated social practice shaped by utility and professional risk. The study offers insights for developing collaborative professional development programmes that support teachers’ critical and sustainable engagement with GenAI.

items.title: Generative AI for Establishing the Chief Complaint
items.abstract: Establishing the chief complaint requires identifying the patient’s main symptoms or concerns. This information is essential for triage and subsequent clinical assessment. However, patients may struggle to describe their symptoms or leave important concerns unspoken. Also, clinicians have limited time to ask further questions during intake. Generative AI could help by asking patients what is troubling them, when their symptoms began, and what other concerns they have. It could prepare a short summary for patients to correct and clinicians to review. Clinical studies of AI-assisted intake have reported shorter physician consultations and more complete recorded histories. These findings do not show whether AI helps clinicians establish the chief complaint more accurately. We propose an evaluation framework centered on the proportion of patients whose main symptoms or concerns are missing or incorrectly described after AI-assisted intake. Studies should compare what patients wanted to discuss with what the AI agent asked about and included in its summary. They should also examine whether concerns requiring urgent assessment were missed. The clinical goal is a clear description of the patient’s main symptoms and concerns that helps clinicians judge urgency and decide what needs attention.

items.title: Generative AI in Distance Education: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for Personalization, Inclusion and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is creating new possibilities for distance education through conversational learning support, personalised explanations, automated feedback and multilingual assistance. However, its integration also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, unequal access, information reliability, learner autonomy and data privacy. This paper develops a conceptual framework for integrating GenAI into distance education through a human-in-the-loop approach. Drawing on relevant scholarly literature and international educational policy documents, the study examines the relationship between AI-supported personalisation, inclusive learning, human oversight and academic accountability. It proposes an integrated framework in which teachers and learners retain meaningful decision-making authority while AI provides supplementary educational support. The framework comprises five dimensions: human agency, equitable access, learner-centred personalisation, academic integrity and responsible data governance. The paper argues that technological availability alone cannot guarantee educational improvement; effective implementation also requires AI literacy, appropriate assessment practices, institutional policies and continuous human evaluation. The proposed framework offers conceptual guidance for higher-education institutions seeking to adopt GenAI responsibly in distance-learning environments. As a conceptual contribution, it requires subsequent empirical evaluation to establish its applicability across different educational contexts.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI MARKETING AND PURCHASE INTENTION AMONG GENERATION Z: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF BRAND PERCEPTION
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping digital marketing by enabling personalised, scalable, and innovative content, while simultaneously raising concerns regarding authenticity and consumer trust. This study examines how Perceived Authenticity, Perceived Personalization, and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation influence Brand Perception and Purchase Intention among Generation Z consumers, with Brand Perception serving as a mediating mechanism. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed using data from 425 Generation Z consumers collected through a structured questionnaire based on five-point Likert-type scales. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson and Spearman correlations, multiple regression, variance inflation factors, HC3 robust standard errors, and bootstrapped mediation analysis based on 5,000 resamples. The findings indicate that Perceived Authenticity (β = .234), Perceived Personalization (β = .160), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .407) significantly and positively influence Brand Perception. Brand Perception significantly predicts Purchase Intention (β = .520). Significant indirect effects were observed for Perceived Authenticity (β = .122), Perceived Personalization (β = .083), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .212) through Brand Perception. The findings demonstrate that consumer responses to GenAI marketing translate into purchase intention substantially through broader brand evaluations. The study highlights the importance of combining AI-enabled innovation and personalization with authenticity and consistent brand positioning.

items.title: Generative AI Use and Learning Productivity Among Google Gemini Users in Bangladesh: An Integrated TAM-Self-Regulated Learning Model
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p < .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p < .001) and PU (β = .218, p < .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p < .001) and SRL (β = .202, p < .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

items.title: Generative AI Use and the Student Well-Being Paradox in Higher Education: Efficiency-Gain Retention, Performance Escalation, and Relative Competition
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce the time and cognitive effort required for university learning, yet technical efficiency does not necessarily translate into improved student well-being. This article develops and tests a conversion account of this paradox by distinguishing efficiency gains that remain available as student-controlled resources from gains that are associated with perceived increases in performance expectations, competitive pressure, verification work, and dependence. A sequential three-study mixed-methods program was conducted with undergraduates in Jiangxi Province. Study 1 used codebook thematic analysis of 42 interviews to identify six mechanisms linking immediate efficiency to resource retention or perceived pressure. Study 2 surveyed 1268 students across eight universities. GenAI use was strongly associated with perceived efficiency gains, but also with perceived performance-standard escalation and verification burden. Positive retention and negative competition pathways were similar in magnitude, yielding a nonsignificant total association with well-being; working-time retention strengthened the efficiency–well-being association. Because Study 2 was cross-sectional, these pathways are interpreted as indirect associations rather than causal mediation. Study 3 used a 2 × 2 experiment (N = 320) and found that AI access improved task quality and reduced completion time under both performance-norm conditions, whereas gains in autonomy, retained time, and state well-being were evident under the stable norm but not statistically distinguishable from zero under the escalated norm. The findings distinguish technical affordance from context-dependent conversion and suggest that responsible AI integration should consider whether efficiency gains remain available for learning, recovery, and student-directed use alongside productivity.

items.title: Generative AI-Guided Versus Human-Guided Learning from Errors in Higher Education: A Comparison of Student Perceptions
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support programming education, but its use in learning-from-errors activities has received limited research attention. This quasi-experimental study compared AI-guided and human-guided support in a structured learning-from-errors programming activity, focusing on students’ perceptions and their variability. A total of 59 college students completed the JavaScript error-detection and correction activity under AI-guided or human-guided support. Following the activity, students completed a questionnaire measuring perceived learning experience, satisfaction, general motivation, self-regulated learning (SRL), and self-efficacy. Between-group differences were examined using Mann–Whitney U tests, and differences in variability were examined using Levene’s tests. Students in the AI-guided condition reported significantly more positive learning experiences and greater satisfaction than those in the human-guided condition. They also reported significantly higher overall SRL and greater use of SRL strategies. No significant differences were found in general motivation, SRL motivation, SRL planning and organization, or self-efficacy. The AI-guided group showed significantly lower raw variability in satisfaction and self-efficacy. However, a sensitivity analysis did not establish that these variance differences remained after accounting for mean-related constraints on the bounded response scale. The findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a scaffold for error analysis when integrated in ways that maintain students’ active cognitive engagement.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence supporting learning and research competency development among postgraduate nursing students: a scoping review
items.abstract: This project documents the methods and analytical framework of a scoping review examining how generative artificial intelligence is used to support learning and research competency development among postgraduate nursing students. The review focuses on six competency domains: information literacy and evidence retrieval, evidence-based practice competency, research methodology and analytical skills, academic writing and scientific communication, critical thinking and research thinking, and AI literacy and responsible AI use. Study selection and data charting were completed before OSF registration; therefore, the registration is intended to provide a transparent record of the review methods rather than a prospective preregistration.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence: Ethical Considerations and Its Impact on Students’ Cognitive Skills
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, influencing how students learn, produce knowledge, and engage in assessments. This study examines the ethical implications of AI integration in university courses and its perceived impact on students’ cognitive skills. Using a mixed-methods secondary data analysis, survey data from 23,218 students across 109 countries and 252 teachers from China, Romania, India, and Brunei were analyzed to explore perceptions of AI capabilities, ethical boundaries, behavioral intentions, and cognitive outcomes. The results have shown that although students are aware of the potential of AI in improving the efficiency and content creation and assistance in the learning process, there are still concerns about overdependence, plagiarism, and lack of critical thinking. The views of faculty underline moral direction and the necessity of systematic assimilation. Developing upon these insights, a theoretical framework is developed that connects antecedent variables, behavior intentions and institutional context to two outcomes the cognitive impact and institutional influence. This framework offers a guide on how universities should introduce generative AI in a responsible manner, and strike a balance between ethical principles and training higher-order cognitive abilities.

items.title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
items.abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On Tülu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.

items.title: GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.

items.title: Geotechnical Instrumentation Plan
items.abstract: A Geotechnical Instrumentation Plan defines the objectives, scope, and methodology for monitoring the behavior of the ground and structures to manage risk throughout a mining project. Its purpose is to translate a site’s hazard and performance criteria into a targeted array of sensors, data collection procedures, alarm thresholds, and response actions. This chapter details a step-by-step process for creating a site-specific instrumentation plan, from initial site investigation and failure-mode analysis to instrument selection, siting, and data protocols. Key elements are discussed in depth: identification of monitoring goals, selection of parameters and sensor t ypes, spatial density and redundancy requirements, and determination of sampling frequency. We outline the contents of an Operation, Maintenance, and Surveillance (OMS) manual, including roles and responsibilities, data protocols, alarm matrices, and escalation procedures (with example tables). Worked design examples illustrate instrument spacing and telemetry design calculations with equations. Comparative tables recommend instrument choices for common scenarios (open-pit walls, underground workings, tailings dams, mine rail). Guidance is provided on procurement, installation, commissioning, and verification of instruments, as well as data management, cybersecurity, and archival practices. Cost and complexity considerations are addressed qualitatively. Three concise case studies (e.g., tailings dam incidents) highlight practical lessons. Finally, common pitfalls and mitigation strategies are summarized, and checklists/templates are presented in table form for field teams. This chapter emphasizes standards-based practice: International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM’s) Global Tailings Standard and Good Practice Guide call for rigorous site-specific monitoring plans. Throughout, we cite recent official and scholarly sources to support the guidance.

items.title: Global Genomic Surveillance of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus
items.abstract: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a persistent zoonotic and epidemic threat. We analyzed 807 publicly available human- and camel-derived MERS-CoV genomes collected during 2012-2024 to assess global genomic surveillance. Most sequences originated from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Major gaps in surveillance persist across Africa and South and Central Asia despite large camel populations, active trade, and evidence of viral circulation. Phylogenetic analysis confirmed predominance of clade B in the Arabian Peninsula and clade C in East Africa, consistent with regional patterns. We identified uneven sampling, incomplete metadata, and long delays between sample collection and public sequence submission, often spanning years. Those limitations reduce the value of genomic data for timely situational awareness. Integrating genomic with population and trade data supports timelier, more representative, and coordinated One Health surveillance for MERS-CoV but reveals major blind spots.

items.title: Governing Generative AI in Higher Education: A Cross-National Analysis of Policy Framing and Student Maneuvering
items.abstract: Universities promote generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a pedagogical resource while regulating it as a risk to academic integrity and fair assessment. This study examines how differentiated policy framing varies across substantive policy dimensions and national contexts, and how students interpret and navigate such guidance in practice. Using a convergent mixed-methods design with quantitative priority, we analyzed GenAI policy documents from 36 universities in Denmark, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the Netherlands, complemented by eight semi-structured interviews with graduate students at one sampled university. Aspect-based sentiment analysis and mixed-effects modeling show significantly positive sentiment in teaching-related statements and significantly negative sentiment in GenAI- and ethics-related statements, while student- and assessment-related statements do not differ significantly from neutral. Neither country nor the policy-dimension-by-country interaction is statistically significant. The interviews contextualize these policy-level patterns: participants described uncertainty around acceptable use, disclosure, and instructor expectations, with responses ranging from cautious experimentation to avoidance. Together, the findings show how differentiated GenAI guidance can coexist within university policy and illustrate the interpretive demands students may face when applying such guidance in practice. Clearer programme- and course-level guidance, consistent disclosure expectations, and stronger support for GenAI literacy may help connect institutional policy more closely with teaching and learning practice.

items.title: Government Support, AI Adoption, and SME Innovation Performance: An Institutional Theory Perspective
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly central to innovation in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), yet resource constraints limit their ability to exploit it. Governments worldwide provide institutional support to encourage SME AI adoption, but whether such support translates into innovation depends on internal organizational conditions that remain poorly understood. Drawing on institutional theory, this study treats government support as a source of coercive, normative, and mimetic pressure and develops an integrative conceptual model in which it influences SME innovation performance through AI adoption intensity, with organizational learning capability as a mediator and organizational readiness as a moderator. The model specifies that government support raises adoption intensity, which in turn enhances innovation performance; that organizational learning capability partially mediates this effect; and that organizational readiness strengthens the link between government support and adoption intensity. A quantitative, cross-sectional design is proposed: structured questionnaires will collect no fewer than 200 valid responses from SMEs, analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Theoretically, the study is expected to extend institutional theory from the adoption/non-adoption dichotomy to a continuous adoption-intensity construct and to position organizational learning as the channel transmitting adoption into innovation. Practically, it can inform the design of differentiated government policy and SME capability building.

items.title: Graph-Based Orchestration of Heterogeneous AI Models: A Control Node Approach to Composite Intelligence
items.abstract: We present a graph-based framework for Composite AI systems that integrate multiple AI techniques to address complex problems. We describe an architecture using specialized control nodes to orchestrate diverse models including planning, machine learning, constraint programming, and large language models. The system employs directed acyclic graphs and behavior trees to manage model relationships and execution sequencing. Our methodology encompasses data connectors, computational services, and a containerized deployment framework supporting hierarchical, sequential, and concurrent model composition patterns. Through case studies, we demonstrate how this architecture enables the creation of composite systems that leverage the strengths of multiple AI techniques within a unified operational schema, overcoming the limitations of single-model approaches.

items.title: GRASP: Geospatial pixel Reasoning viA Structured Policy learning
items.abstract: Geospatial pixel reasoning aims to generate segmentation masks in optical RGB remote sensing imagery directly from natural-language instructions. Most existing approaches fine-tune a multimodal large language models (MLLM) with dense pixel-level masks as ground truth. While effective within the training distribution, this paradigm suffers from two main drawbacks: (1) the high cost of large-scale dense mask annotation, and (2) the limited generalization capability of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios . To address these issues, we propose G eospatial pixel R easoning vi A S tructured P olicy learning ( GRASP ), a structured policy-learning framework that cascades an MLLM with a pretrained segmentation model. To enhance generalization, we introduce Pure Reinforcement for Instruction-to-Mask Execution ( PRIME ), a training paradigm that replaces SFT with reinforcement learning to better align reasoning and grounding behaviors with task objectives. To reduce annotation costs, we design Box-and-Points Rewards ( BoP-Rewards ), which substitute dense mask labels with bounding boxes and positive points. BoP-Rewards evaluate model outputs through two complementary signals: format, which constrains the reasoning and grounding structure to remain syntactically parsable, and accuracy, which measures the quality of predicted boxes and points. Our experiments focus on 3-channel optical RGB imagery from public remote sensing datasets. We train GRASP and all baselines on EarthReason and GeoPixInstruct, and construct an in-domain benchmark by merging their test sets. We further release GRASP -1k, a fully OOD benchmark with reasoning-intensive queries, reasoning traces, and fine-grained masks. Experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art in-domain performance and a 54% relative improvement in OOD gIoU over GeoPix, the strongest competing baseline on this metric. These results confirm that reinforcement learning with cost-aware rewards provides a robust and scalable paradigm for geospatial pixel reasoning. All code and datasets will be released publicly.
